Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are oxygen-derived molecules produced naturally by cells and by environmental factors. At controlled levels, they help regulate cell signaling and immune defenses, when they build up faster than antioxidant systems can remove them, they can damage DNA, proteins, and fats (lipid peroxidation), a state called oxidative stress.

In chemistry and biology, ROS are highly reactive chemical species formed from diatomic oxygen (O2), water radiolysis, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Some prominent ROS are the hydroperoxide radical or hydroperoxyl (HO2•), its deprotonated form, the superoxide anion (O2•−), the hydroxyl radical (HO•), and singlet oxygen (1O2).

ROS are pervasive because they are readily produced from O2, which is abundant in the Earth's atmosphere (21 vol%) and is present in the dissolved state in biological fluids (O2 solubility in water ~2×10, 4 mol/L).
